entries.name: Character Creation Guide
entries.text: This guide can be used for Players or Dungeon Masters new to the Dungeons and Devil Fruits System. It should be noted that all steps marked with DM’s Choice are optional and do not need to be followed. Those rules are there to bring the system more in line with the setting and provide players with additional tools for their character.

sections.name: Step 1: Choose a Devil Fruit or Haki (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
Begin your character by selecting either a Devil Fruit or Haki to shape your character’s unique abilities with your DM’s help.
Devil Fruits. These powerful, rare fruits grant incredible abilities, but at the cost of the eater’s ability to swim. If you choose a Devil Fruit, consult Chapter 7 of the Dungeons and Devil Fruits Player’s Handbook, the Dungeons and Devil Expanded Fruits Devil Fruit Encyclopedia, or Chapter 6 of this Handbook. Your DM will guide you, either rolling on a generation table for a randomized choice or allowing you to pick a specific fruit.
Haki. Even if you do not consume a Devil Fruit, you may still increase your prowess with Haki over the course of your adventures. In Chapter 5 of this Handbook, you’ll find options to develop this innate power.
For extra potential, roll for “Qualities of a King” in the Color of the Supreme King Advancement section to determine if you possess this rare Haki type.

sections.name: Step 2: Determine Devil Fruit Scaling (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
The power of a Devil Fruit can grow and evolve over time, adding new layers of depth and strength to your character’s abilities. However, whether your Devil Fruit scales as you progress is up to the DM’s discretion. DMs can refer to Chapter 6 of this Handbook to decide if they want to use scaling rules for Devil Fruits.
This choice affects how your Devil Fruit abilities unfold through your journey, whether they remain consistent or expand in impact as your character grows.

sections.name: Step 3: Determine Universal Features (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, characters possess remarkable endurance that allow them to face incredible challenges and keep fighting. To reflect this in gameplay, DMs can choose to apply Universal Features from Chapter 1 of this Handbook.
These features provide characters with durability that aligns more closely with the One Piece universe, giving players the sense of pushing their limits just like the iconic characters of the series.

sections.name: Step 4: Determine Special Reactions (DM’s Choice)
sections.text:
One Piece combat is fast-paced, dynamic, and full of surprises, where quick reflexes often turn the tide of battle. To capture this spirit, DMs can introduce Special Reactions from Chapter 1 of this Handbook.
These special reactions provide characters with additional ways to respond to threats, creating a more versatile combat experience in line with the series.

sections.name: Step 5: Choose a Race
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, countless unique races inhabit the seas, each with their own distinct traits and abilities. Players can explore these options in Chapter 2: Character Races.
When choosing a race, make sure to also select a subrace if one is available, as it adds another layer of individuality to your character.

sections.name: Step 6: Choose a Class
sections.text: Your class defines your character’s core skills and combat style within the crew. Classes and Subclasses can be found in Chapter 3: Character Classes.

sections.name: Step 7: Determine Ability Scores
sections.text:
Much of what your character does in the game depends on his or her six abilities: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. Each ability has a score, which is a number you record on your character sheet.
The six abilities and their use in the game are described in the Using Ability Scores section. The Ability Score Summary table provides a quick reference for what qualities are measured by each ability, what races increase which abilities, and what classes consider each ability particularly important.
You generate your character’s six ability scores randomly. Roll four 6-sided dice and record the total of the highest three dice on a piece of scratch paper. Do this five more times, so that you have six numbers. If you want to save time or don’t like the idea of randomly determining ability scores, you can use the following scores instead: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8.
Now take your six numbers and write each number beside one of your character’s six abilities to assign scores to Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma. Afterward, make any changes to your ability scores as a result of your race choice.
After assigning your ability scores, determine your ability modifiers using the Ability Scores and Modifiers table. To determine an ability modifier without consulting the table, subtract 10 from the ability score and then divide the result by 2 (round down). Write the modifier next to each of your scores.

sections.name: Step 8: Pick a Background
sections.text: Your background provides insight into your character’s past, skills, and motivations, helping to shape who they are beyond their combat abilities. Backgrounds can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook, offering a variety of options, from archaeologist to noble, each with unique skills, proficiencies, and starting equipment.

sections.name: Step 9: Pick Your Crew Role
sections.text:
Every member of a pirate crew plays a vital part in its success, and your crew role will define how you contribute to the ship’s journey. Crew roles can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook. Each role provides unique abilities and proficiencies.
Only one player can occupy each crew role, ensuring that every crewmate brings something distinct to the adventure. Choose a role that aligns with your character’s strengths and aspirations.

sections.name: Step 10: Choose Equipment
sections.text:
Your class and background determine your character’s starting equipment, including weapons, armor, and other adventuring gear. Record this equipment on your character sheet. All such items are detailed in Chapter 5 of the Dungeons and Devil Fruits Player’s Handbook.
Your Strength score limits the amount of gear you can carry. Try not to purchase equipment with a total weight (in pounds) exceeding your Strength score times 15. “Using Ability Scores” has more information on carrying capacity.

sections.name: Step 11: Describe your Character
sections.text: Once you know the basic game aspects of your character, it’s time to flesh them out as a person. Your character needs a name. Spend a few minutes thinking about what they look like and how they behave in general terms.

sections.name: Step 12: Create a Backstory and Dream
sections.text:
In the world of One Piece, every pirate has a story and a dream that fuels their journey. Now it’s time to bring your character to life by crafting their backstory and defining the dream that pushes them forward. Example dreams can be found in Chapter 1 of this Handbook, but for a more personal touch, creating your own unique dream is encouraged.
Consider what has driven your character to join the crew. Did they experience hardship or adventure that ignited their desire for freedom or power? What do they hope to achieve? A dream could be as grand as finding the One Piece or as personal as reuniting with a lost family. Let this vision guide your character’s choices, as it is the heart of their story and will inspire them as they face the challenges of the open sea.

sections.name: Join your Crew!
sections.text: With your character ready, it’s time to set sail and join your crew on a grand adventure! You’ve crafted a unique individual with their own strengths, dreams, and purpose, and now they’re ready to face the vast unknown. Have fun!

entries.name: Universal Features
entries.text: Universal features give the players of your game main character plot armor. So if you want to push the One Piece vibe, take these.

sections.name: Dream Points
sections.text: A character starts with 1 dream point at 1st Level. Each time the character gains a level, they lose any unspent dream points and gain a new total equal to the character’s level. A player can spend a dream point whenever they make an Attack roll, an ability check, or a saving throw. The player can spend the dream point after the roll is made but before any of its results are applied. Spending the dream point allows the player to roll a d6 and add it to The D20, possibly turning a failure into a success. In addition, whenever a character fails a death saving throw, the player can spend one dream point to turn the failure into a success.

sections.name: I Won’t Abandon My Dreams
sections.text: As you lay bloody and dying at the feet of your enemy, your memories and dreams rush through your mind giving you hope. If at any point you reach 0 hit points and you die, instead roll a d20, on a 12 or higher you stand back up and regain 1 hp. If you died because you reached exhaustion level 6, instead go back to exhaustion level 5.

sections.name: Healing Surge
sections.text:
As an action or bonus action (DM Discretion), a character can healing surge and spend up to half his or her Hit Dice (minimum 1). For each Hit Die spent in this way, the player rolls the die and adds the character’s Constitution modifier. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.
A character who uses a healing surge can’t do so again until he or she finishes a short or long rest.
A character regains all spent Hit Dice at the end of a long rest.

entries.name: Special Reactions
entries.text:
Special Reactions are a unique type of reaction that players can use to enhance their combat effectiveness and bring a dynamic, One Piece-inspired flair to the game.
These reactions are separate from normal reactions and are designed to reflect the tactical maneuvers seen in the series.
Each player gets 2 Special Reactions a combat round and can use each Special Reaction a number of times equal to their proficiency bonus per short rest. The Special Reactions are as followed:

sections.name: Counter Strike
sections.text: When an enemy misses an attack against the player, the player may use their special reaction to make a melee or ranged weapon attack against the attacker.

sections.name: Deflect Projectile
sections.text: When an enemy makes a ranged attack roll against the player and it hits, the player may use their special reaction to reduce the damage by 1d10 + their player level.

sections.name: Flash Step
sections.text: When an enemy makes a successful attack roll against the player but before the damage is dealt, the player can use their special reaction to make a Dexterity saving throw against the attacker’s attack roll. If you succeed on the roll, move 10 ft. to an unoccupied space of your choice without provoking opportunity attacks and take no damage from the attack. On a failed save take the full damage of the attack and you may still move 10 ft. in a straight line without provoking opportunity attacks. You cannot use this special reaction if your movement speed is 0.

sections.name: Parry Blow
sections.text: When an enemy hits the player with a melee attack, the player can use their special reaction to reduce the damage by 1d10 + their player level.

sections.name: Shield Bash
sections.text: When an enemy makes an attack roll and hits the player, the player may use their special reaction to make a shield attack if they have a shield equipped, knocking the enemy prone if the attack hits. Shield Attack Melee Weapon Attack: +strength modifier, reach 5 ft., one creature, Hit: 4 (1d4) bludgeoning damage.

entries.name: Inspiration Dice Alternative: Pirate Prestige
entries.text:
In order to understand how crew roles work, it is important to understand a new system of reward points I am introducing called “Pirate Prestige“. This is intended to reward players for playing their roles to the best of their ability, while also promoting proper teamwork. A crew that works together will succeed, and this system is designed to make that process feel very fulfilling. While you can use Inspiration Dice in favor of this system if you don’t like it, it is another easy way to balance crew roles by rewarding points to players, which can be used for strengthening their role’s abilities and different roleplay elements.
The way this works is fairly simple. Whenever players overcome a difficult challenge, like winning a fight against a mighty enemy pirate, battling a deadly storm on the seas, or simply saving a town from danger, everyone who did well in that situation will gain a point of pirate prestige. However, characters that were absent, didn’t want to help the group, or simply complained and caused issues for others shouldn’t receive any points. Fighting pointless battles, intentionally running into dangerous situations which have no reward, or simply trying to farm these points will not net the crew any points. At higher levels, you can also choose to elect an MVP character during an event. Players may decide someone in the crew went above and beyond in overcoming a challenge, and give them a large surge of pirate prestige points at the end of the encounter. An MVP may roll a 1d4 at the end of such an event, and gain a number of pirate prestige points equal to the number rolled. A character can have a maximum number of Pirate Prestige points equal to half their character level, rounded up.

sections.name: Methods of Spending Pirate Prestige
sections.text: While pirate prestige should be primarily used to benefit the crew as a whole and should heavily reward teamwork, it can also be spent in a few other ways. Stockpiling these points can be rewarding and beneficial to overcoming future challenges. Other uses for pirate prestige is described under “Crew Roles” up next, but these points can be used for anything that the DM deems to be fun or appropriate for roleplay, investigating, or exploration, such as the following abilities:

sections.name: Pirate Prestige Ability: Locate Quests
sections.text: When exploring a populated town, city, or village, a character may expend 1 pirate prestige point to locate a random NPC or troubled creature that will provide them with a task to complete (up to the DM to decide the difficulty and reward), without needing to make any skill checks. To use this ability again, a character must complete a long rest.

sections.name: Pirate Prestige Ability: Find Minor Clue
sections.text: If a group is stuck on a mission or quest that they need to complete, a character may expend 1 pirate prestige point to ask the DM for a minor hint or clue that may lead them on the right track. This can only be used once per character during any single mission or quest.

sections.name: Pirate Prestige Ability: Gain Reputation
sections.text: If a group wants to gain recognition or respect in a single kingdom, village or town, or simply undo their negative reputation, characters may spend 24 hours and 1 pirate prestige point to spread rumors and tales of their deeds and gain 1 point of reputation in that location (explained further in the One Piece D&D 5E DM’s guide). A character can only use this ability this way once per location, and a crew can only spend a total of 5 pirate prestige points altogether to gain reputation in a location. A crew cannot use this ability when they only have 1 reputation point in that location.

entries.name: Crew Recruitment
entries.text:
The following rules are optional and intended for groups and DMs who wish to incorporate resource management into their campaign.
For smaller ships, a party of 4–5 adventurers can manage operations with assigned officer roles. However, as the ship grows in size or complexity, additional crew becomes necessary. These supplementary NPCs, known as Hirelings, can be recruited from seafaring communities—especially bustling port cities.
A general rule of thumb is one officer per ten hirelings to maintain discipline and structure. These officers may oversee departments, supervise tasks, or serve as apprentices under player characters. Hirelings can be assigned as assistants (e.g., an assistant chef or assistant navigator), or given basic maintenance and labor tasks.

sections.name: Hireling Wages
sections.text:
Hirelings require fair treatment, food, lodging, and pay. Use the “Recruit” stat block (see DM Cabin for statblock) for base hirelings, or higher CR NPCs for officers and specialists.
Standard Hireling: ฿15,000 per week (฿60,000 per month)
Specialist Officer: ฿150,000 per week (฿600,000 per month)

sections.name: Loyalty & Mutiny
sections.text:
Poor treatment can sow the seeds of rebellion. Every instance of mistreatment—underpayment, neglect, or abuse—adds a cumulative +10 to your weekly loyalty roll that affected hirelings or fleet crews may begin planning a mutiny. Proper compensation or acts of goodwill reduce this chance.
Conversely, hirelings and fleet crews treated with respect may form bonds with the crew and add a cumulative -5 to your weekly loyalty roll. Over time, they may become trusted companions, apprentices, or even receive stat improvements.

sections.name: Loyalty Roll
sections.text: Once per week, the DM will roll a 1d100 on the loyalty role table if you have mistreated any of your crew members.

rows: Happy Crew. Your crew continues to be loyal. Each player gains a Inspiration - Pirate Prestige point.
Dissatisfied Crew. Add +25 to the next loyalty roll.
Mutiny. Roll on the Mutiny Table.
Individual Mutiny. Only the individuals who are wronged on the crew will mutiny.
Small Mutiny. Less than half the crew will mutiny.
Mass Mutiny. More than half the crew will mutiny.
Complete Mutiny. All crew members will mutiny against the players.

sections.name: Fleet Command
sections.text:
As a crew’s notoriety and influence grows, a single ship may no longer suffice. In time, captains may expand their domain by assembling a Fleet.
Rather than tracking every gold coin spent on wages across the fleet, DMs may assume that secondary ships are self-sustaining unless impacted by major events such as plunder, ship damage, or mutiny. Allied ships joining the fleet through alliances may not require wages at all.
Additionally, communication between ships is crucial. Den Den Mushi provide long-distance communication, allowing ships to share intelligence and coordinate attacks.
Flagship. The primary vessel, commanded by the crew’s captain.
Fleet Commanders. Trusted lieutenants (PCs or NPCs) who helm additional ships in the fleet.
Fleet Officers & Crew. Each ship maintains its own officer structure, crew, and operations.

sections.name: Fleet Wages
sections.text: Fleets require upkeep to maintain. Use the table below to determine how much the cost of maintaining your fleet will cost. Do not factor in your own vessel when determining the cost.

sections.name: Fleet Orders
sections.text: Fleet commanders may embark on side missions or independent expeditions under orders from the captain. When a fleet vessel ventures off alone, the DM rolls on the Fleet Event Table each time it reaches a new island or region. They arrive at said islands every time the Flagship reaches one in their travels.

rows: Grow Influence. The fleet spreads your flag across the island, granting your influence over the territory. The Flagship gains passive income from the region, adding ฿200,000 per week to the players earnings for every island in their territory.
Plunder. The fleet finds enough bellies to pay for the fleet’s
Warded Off. The fleet was not able to make their way inland
and disembarked to a new island.
Fleet Tragedy. Roll on the Fleet Tragedy Table.
Minor Damage. The ship withstands insignificant scratches and dents which can easily be patched over the remaining duration of the trip.
Major Damage. The ship withstands serious damage and the hit points of its hull are reduced by 50% of its maximum
Broken Parts. A random component other than the hull of the ship is completely destroyed during the encounter.
Plague. The crew becomes diseased during the encounter.
Deadly Poison. The crew is poisoned during the encounter.
Captured. The ship and crew are captured by enemies
Launched. The ship and crew are suddenly sprung onto a
nearby sky island and become stranded.
Mysterious Disappearance. The ship and crew drop all
communication during the encounter and the entire crew vanishes for unknown reasons. However, the ship can still be recovered.
Complete Annihilation. The ship is completely destroyed and sinks to the bottom of the ocean along with the crew.

entries.name: Character Dreams
entries.text:
To keep players invested and eagerly rushing to the table each session, especially if this is a long-running campaign, it is key to give motivation to every player and character. The most powerful motivator may come in the form of an individual character’s dream. This dream could be something vague or extremely difficult to achieve. Regardless, it should be something that becomes more and more feasible to accomplish and characters advance throughout the story and grow stronger.
For example, a character may dream of creating the greatest pirate ship the world has ever seen. As the story progresses, the crew may gather more materials and wealth to upgrade the ship, slowly allowing for this character’s dream to come to fruition. Accomplishing this dream toward the end of the story is important, but it is far more imperative to drive the player and character’s ambition throughout the journey to build up to such a grand dream being accomplished.
For a player to determine what their character’s dream may be, it is a good idea to pull from that character’s race, class, crew role, background, ideals, or bonds to develop a fitting dream. This dream should be overarching and overshadow any other less important bonds or objectives your character has. Alternatively, you may choose an option from the table below or roll to decide what your character’s dream will be. You can have multiple dreams or combine them together.

rows: 2d20 Example Character Dream 2 To become the greatest of your race or occupation 3 To research every type of plant or animal 4 To spread your ideals or religion to every nation 5 To find a certain type of powerful Devil Fruit 6 To tame every type of monster in the world 7 To become the wealthiest person alive 8 To restore absolute justice to the world 9 To reach the moon or a certain planet 10 To defeat the Navy or World Government 11 To uncover a lost civilization 12 To bring peace and unity between your race and others 13 To find an old friend or family member 14 To build the ultimate ship that will sail the world 15 To uncover the true history of the world 16 To surpass a legendary person or creature 17 To become a brave warrior of the sea 18 To become the strongest fighter or swordsman 19 To map out the entire planet 20 To find the One Piece and become Pirate King 21 To create a floating island or city 22 To collect every type of rare artifact or treasure 23 To cure an incurable disease 24 To write the most famous book in history 25 To become a legendary chef known across the seas 26 To build a kingdom where no one suffers 27 To explore every island in the Grand Line 28 To awaken and master all forms of Haki 29 To avenge a fallen crew or loved one 30 To live forever and witness the world’s future 31 To host the world’s greatest tournament 32 To craft the world’s strongest weapon 33 To have your name etched into history forever 34 To save a dying species or ecosystem 35 To bring down the Celestial Dragons 36 To master every known style of combat 37 To steal from every major world power 38 To find and raise a legendary sea king 39 To visit the ends of the world and return 40 To laugh at the end of the world, no matter what

entries.name: Multiclassing & Starting Wealth
entries.text: Because these classes haven’t been thoroughly tested and balanced for multiclassing, it is possible that multiclassing may break some of the game balance in a campaign. If you still insist on doing so, here are the the rules, prerequisites, and proficiencies you will gain from multiclassing using classes in this pdf.

sections.name: Prerequisites
sections.text: To qualify for a new class, you must have a score of at least 13 in the primary ability of the new class and your current classes. For example, a bruiser who decides to multiclass into the skald class must have both Strength and Charisma scores of 13 or higher. Without the full training that a beginning character receives, you must be a quick study in your new class, having a natural aptitude that is reflected by higher-than-average ability scores.

sections.name: Starting Wealth
sections.text:
Every character starts with a selection of equipment and adventuring gear in their inventory. When creating your character, after selecting your class and background, you may decide to start with the equipment listed in your class’s starting equipment or start with a set amount of Belly (฿) to spend on equipment of your choice listed in this chapter.
If you opt to forgo taking your class’s starting equipment, you may roll the amount of starting wealth you have on the table below based on your class. Then, buy any amount of equipment you’d like from the stores listed in this chapter, not including exotic or black market equipment.

sections.name: Experience Points
sections.text: The experience point cost to gain a level is always based on your total character level, as shown in the Character Advancement table, not your level in a particular class.

sections.name: Hit Points and Hit Dice
sections.text:
You gain the Hit Points from your new class as described for levels after 1. You gain the level 1 Hit Points for a class only when your total character level is 1.
Add together the Hit Dice granted by all your classes to form your pool of Hit Dice. If these dice are the same die type, you can pool them together.

sections.name: Proficiency Bonus
sections.text: Your proficiency bonus is always based on your total character level, not your level in a particular class.

sections.name: Starting Proficiencies
sections.text: When you gain your first level in a class other than your initial class, you gain all of new class’s starting armor, weapon, and tool proficiencies.

sections.name: Class Features
sections.text: When you gain a new level in a class, you get its features for that level. You don’t, however, receive the class’s starting equipment, and a few features have additional rules when you’re multiclassing: Channel Divinity, Extra Attack, Unarmored Defense, and Spellcasting.

sections.name: Channel Divinity
sections.text: If you already have the Channel Divinity feature and gain a level in a class that also grants the feature, you gain the Channel Divinity effects granted by that class, but getting the feature again doesn’t give you an additional use of it. You gain additional uses only when you reach a class level that explicitly grants them to you.

sections.name: Extra Attack
sections.text: If you gain the Extra Attack class feature from more than one class, the features don’t add together. You can’t make more than two attacks with this feature unless it says you do (as the warrior’s version of Extra Attack does).

sections.name: Armor Class
sections.text: If you have multiple ways to calculate your Armor Class, you can benefit from only one at a time.

sections.name: Spellcasting
sections.text:
Your capacity for spellcasting depends partly on your combined levels in all your spellcasting classes and partly on your individual levels in those classes. Once you have the Spellcasting feature from more than one class, use the rules below. If you multiclass but have the Spellcasting feature from only one class, you follow the rules as described in that class.
Spells Known and Prepared. You determine what spells you know and can prepare for each class individually, as if you were a single-classed member of that class.
Each spell you know and prepare is associated with one of your classes, and you use the spellcasting ability of that class when you cast the spell. Similarly, a spellcasting focus, such as a holy symbol, can be used only for the spells from the class associated with that focus.
Spell Slots. You determine your available spell slots by adding together all your levels in the priest, skald, and tinkerer classes. Use this total to determine your spell slots by consulting the Multiclass Spellcaster table.
If you have more than one spellcasting class, this table might give you spell slots of a level that is higher than the spells you know or can prepare. You can use those slots, but only to cast your lower-level spells. If a lower-level spell that you cast, like burning hands, has an enhanced effect when cast using a higher-level slot, you can use the enhanced effect, even though you don’t have any spells of that higher level.

entries.name: Alternative Multiclassing Rules
entries.text:
Many multiclass options may break campaigns due to the nature of this setting. If a DM does not wish to allow Multiclassing due to the power scaling of characters with multiple classes, they may apply these rules for a more balanced game.
With these rules, multiclassing is no longer available. A character cannot take levels in more than one class.
Instead, change the Borrow Skill spiritual surge, found in Chapter 5: Spirit Surges - Standard Surge Advancement, to the following:

sections.name: Borrow Skill
sections.text:
Standard Advancement, Uncommon
Learn a single feature from a class or subclass of your choice. You cannot pick a feature that is a higher level than your current character level.
The class feature and/or subclass feature can not be from any class you currently have levels in and you cannot grab a feature that grants spell slots.
This advancement can be chosen up to three times.
